story:
The Tennessee Urban Forestry Council says this willow oak was already standing when the Bonny Oaks Orphanage opened in 1854 to teach children farming on a working farm. By the council's reckoning that makes it more than 170 years old. Wikipedia, more cautiously, says over 100 years, and calls it the oldest tree in an arboretum of 55 species.

The ground has changed hands around it. It was Cherokee land before Colonel Lewis Shepherd settled the area. Colonel Jarrett G. Dent built the house behind the tree in 1840, and the Dent House is now on the National Register of Historic Places. In 1867 Captain C. C. Peak named the place Bonnie Oaks for the stately oaks around the homestead. Whether this oak was one of the trees he meant, nobody wrote down.

The council named it a Historic Tree in 2000. The Dent House is now the Hamilton County Agriculture Center, and the arboretum in front of it is a small round park on county land, free and open every day, on the north-east side of Chattanooga about 10 miles from downtown.

Nobody has published its girth or its height. If you go with a tape measure, tell us what you find, and if you know of other old trees in Chattanooga worth the walk, tell us about those too.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its narrow, willow-like leaves, unusual on an oak. It stands in the small round Bonny Oaks Arboretum in front of the Dent House, 6183 Adamson Circle.
name: Bonny Oaks Willow Oak

location.address: Bonny Oaks Arboretum, 6183 Adamson Circle, Chattanooga, TN 37416 (in front of the Dent House, now the Hamilton County Agriculture Center)

official_register.name: Tennessee Urban Forestry Council Landmark, Historic & Heritage Tree Registry (Historic Tree, 2000)

access: Free; Bonny Oaks Arboretum is a small round park open daily without charge (Wikipedia). It sits on Hamilton County Parks land.
transport: No public transport verified; the site is on the north-east side of Chattanooga, about 10 miles from downtown.
verify_notes: TUFC register: the willow oak stands in Hamilton County on land once occupied by the Cherokee. Colonel Lewis Shepherd settled the area; Colonel Jarrett G. Dent built the Dent House (National Register) in 1840; Captain C.C. Peak named the place Bonnie Oaks in 1867 for the stately oaks around the homestead. The register says the tree dates to before 1854, when the Bonny Oaks Orphanage was established to teach agrarian skills on a working farm. Historic Tree 2000, nominated by Kelly Jackson. Tree is on Hamilton County Parks property. Age conflict: TUFC says before 1854 (so over about 170 years), Wikipedia describes the willow oak in the arboretum as over 100 years old and the oldest specimen in the 55-species collection. I record the register's date as a lower bound; stated as 'over 170 years' with a flag. The Times Free Press (Dec 2015, a story on the fall of the Baylor red oak) has the city forester calling it one of the few remaining historically significant oaks in the county (that article read via search summary only, not fetched, so that quote is unverified). Pin is the arboretum centre (Nominatim for the address 35.07306,-85.18270), not the trunk: the arboretum is a small round park so a visitor will find the largest oak. Alive: TUFC entry modified 2026-01-22; lifecheck RECENT (iNaturalist 2025-10-13 within 100 m of the arboretum, not tied to this trunk). Photo: none found on Commons by geosearch (250 m).

hold: lead quality: one 2022 Times Free Press report whose page returned 404, no measurement, trunks not told apart (US Southeast run 2026-11-04)
name: Grace Episcopal Church Water and Willow Oaks

location.address: Grace Episcopal Church (GreenGrace Arboretum), 20 Belvoir Avenue, Chattanooga, TN 37411

official_register.name: City of Chattanooga Tree Commission, Chattanooga Notable Trees Register (map only, not public)

access: Church grounds on the corner of Brainerd Road and Belvoir Avenue, a tree-covered lawn visible from the street; the arboretum is meant for public visits but no hours were found. Sidewalk to Brainerd Road is still a wish-list item per the church. Treat as view from public ground; confirm before relying on entry.
transport: No public transport verified (CARTA service to Brainerd Road not checked).
verify_notes: ONE SOURCE, Times Free Press 19 Jan 2022 (page returned 404 to my fetch; content known from search results only): the water oak and willow oak are the oldest and tallest specimens on the church property and appear on Chattanooga's Notable Trees Register. The church's arboretum (about 4 acres) was certified a Level Two Arboretum (60+ species) by the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council in December 2021 per the Diocese of East Tennessee event page (73 tree species listed on its legend). No age, girth or height published; which of the two oaks is the willow oak cannot be said, so the entry is for the pair and species is the willow oak by convention. Candidate is weak: list as lead-quality unless the Tree Commission map yields coordinates. Kept because fewer than four is still kept; photo: none found. Location_site candidate: Grace Episcopal churchyard, radius 50 m.
